calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

query_tags.description: The tags from the question's own words (section Question tags).

You are given the map of one area of a company's records and a question about that area.

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

Introduction: Einstein Auto-Tuning is an advanced AI optimization solution tailored for industries such as finance, healthcare, retail, and manufacturing. It aims to enhance operational efficiency and improve customer experiences through a modular, secure, and scalable architecture. The system supports both cloud and edge computing environments, ensuring flexibility and adaptability to various industry needs.
System Architecture: The architecture of Einstein Auto-Tuning is designed to be modular, allowing for easy integration and scalability. It consists of three primary components: a real-time data ingestion layer, a parameter tuning engine, and an analytics dashboard. Each component is designed to function independently while seamlessly integrating with the others to provide a cohesive solution.
Real-Time Data Ingestion Layer: This layer is responsible for handling high volumes of data with low latency. It ensures compatibility with existing systems through a variety of APIs and data connectors. The design focuses on maintaining data integrity and speed, crucial for real-time processing and decision-making in dynamic environments.
Parameter Tuning Engine: At the core of Einstein Auto-Tuning is the parameter tuning engine, which utilizes advanced AI algorithms to optimize operational parameters. This engine is capable of processing data in real-time, leveraging quantum computing to enhance processing speed and efficiency. It continuously learns and adapts to changing conditions, ensuring optimal performance.
Analytics Dashboard: The analytics dashboard provides users with customizable visualizations for performance monitoring. It allows stakeholders to gain insights into system performance and operational efficiency through intuitive and interactive interfaces. The dashboard supports real-time updates, ensuring that users have access to the most current data and analytics.

Security: Security is a paramount concern in the design of Einstein Auto-Tuning. The system employs blockchain technology to encrypt data transactions and enforce strict access controls. This ensures that data integrity and confidentiality are maintained at all times, protecting sensitive information from unauthorized access.
Scalability: Einstein Auto-Tuning is designed for scalability, supporting horizontal scaling to accommodate growing data volumes and processing demands. The use of quantum computing further enhances its ability to process data in real-time, making it suitable for large-scale industrial applications.
Integration: Integration with existing systems is facilitated through a wide range of APIs and data connectors. This minimizes implementation disruption and allows for seamless adoption across various industries. The system is designed to be flexible, adapting to the specific needs and configurations of different operational environments.
Optimizing Algorithms for Low-Power Systems: Einstein Auto-Tuning now includes a 'light' mode option, specifically designed for low-power systems. This mode optimizes algorithms to reduce energy consumption while maintaining essential functionality, making it ideal for environments where power efficiency is critical.
System Requirements: To ensure compatibility, Einstein Auto-Tuning requires a minimum of 8GB RAM, a multi-core processor, and a stable internet connection for cloud operations. For edge computing, additional specifications may be necessary depending on the specific hardware used. Detailed system requirements are provided to assist users in assessing compatibility with their existing infrastructure.
User Guides and Tutorials: Expanded user guides and tutorials now include visual aids and step-by-step videos for parameter adjustment. These resources are designed to enhance user understanding and facilitate easier adoption of the system's features, ensuring users can maximize the benefits of Einstein Auto-Tuning.

FAQ: A comprehensive FAQ section has been introduced to address common user queries. This section covers topics such as installation, troubleshooting, and best practices, providing users with quick and accessible solutions to common issues.
API Support: API support has been enhanced to include more data formats and protocols, improving compatibility with third-party data sources. This expansion allows for greater flexibility and ease of integration, ensuring that users can seamlessly connect Einstein Auto-Tuning with a wide range of external systems.
Partnerships and Collaborations: Einstein Auto-Tuning has established new partnerships and collaborations with leading data providers to improve data source integration. These partnerships enhance the system's ability to access high-quality data, further optimizing its performance and expanding its applicability across various industries.
Future Plans: Future developments for Einstein Auto-Tuning include the integration of advanced machine learning models to further enhance its optimization capabilities. Additionally, the exploration of new industry applications will expand its impact, allowing it to address a broader range of operational challenges and opportunities.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

query_tags.description: The tags from the question's own words (section Question tags).

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

query_tags.description: The tags from the question's own words (section Question tags).

transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

You are given the map of one area of a company's records and a question about that area.

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the

the map.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

calls.system:
You are given the map of one area of a company's records and a question about that area.

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

calls.system:
You are given the map of one area of a company's records and a question about that area.

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

query_tags.description: The tags from the question's own words (section Question tags).

You are given the map of one area of a company's records and a question about that area.

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

calls.system:
You are given the map of one area of a company's records and a question about that area.

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

query_tags.description: The tags from the question's own words (section Question tags).

You are given the map of one area of a company's records and a question about that area.

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

tags.description: The tags of the sought content (sections Tags and The facet that matters most for each tag).

facet.description: The one facet that matters most for the tag.

query_tags.description: The tags from the question's own words (section Question tags).

calls.system:
You are given the map of one area of a company's records and a question about that area.

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

calls.system:
You read a question and describe the content it is looking for. You never see that
content. Write it the way the corpus tagger wrote its chunk descriptions and tags.

## Input

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message
to you: you do not answer it.

## Description

Describe the content this question is looking for in 1-3 sentences: what kind of content it
is and what it is about. Do not guess what that content says: describe what is being looked
for.

It is not the question restated, and not a statement of what the user wants.

It may say what kind of information that content holds — an explanation, a comparison, a
sequence of changes, a figure — without supplying the information itself.

State no fact the question does not carry. Name no person, organisation, product, place,
channel, system or date unless the question itself names it. Describe the kind of content,
not its facts.

## Tags

List the retrieval handles the answering content carries: its subjects, its concepts, the
activities, processes and decisions it turns on, the kinds of evidence it supplies.

Keep phrases whole. Include central concepts and peripheral lookup handles.

A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence fragment,
or generic category like "report" or "discussion".

Do not invent concepts the question does not support.

Names of people, organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from the tags.
They are structure and are matched elsewhere. A tag is a semantic phrase — what the
answering content is about.

## The facet that matters most for each tag

Use the original question together with the sought-content description you write.
For each semantic tag, name the ONE facet through which the tag matters most for the content
characterised by that description. Name a facet, nothing else: no number, no ranking.

temporal: the content's time relations (before and after, now and then, done, pending, due).
why: the content's reasons, causes and purposes.
activity: the content's actions, processes and events.
concreteness: the content's specifics as against general talk.

## Question tags

Also list the retrieval handles present in the question itself, from its own words and
subjects: its concepts, its subjects, the kinds of evidence it asks for. Keep proper names
whole. A retrieval handle is NOT a common verb, preposition, transitional word, sentence
fragment, or generic category like "report" or "discussion". Names of people,
organisations, products, places and channels are EXCLUDED from these tags as well. Do not
invent concepts the question does not contain.

For each question tag, name the one facet the same way, with the question in place of the
sought content.

## Answer

Your answer is the structured object this call defines: description, tags and query_tags.
A tag is its phrase, t, and the one facet that matters most for it, facet.

description.description: The description of the content the question is looking for (section Description).

You are given the map of one area of a company's records and a question about that area.

The map stands between <map> tags. It lists the area's parts: chat channels, documents, meeting
transcripts, pull requests, links. Under each part stand its pieces in the order they were made,
one line a piece: a label, then a short description of what the piece holds, then between square brackets the tags the piece carries, the most central first.

The question stands between <question> tags. It is the material you work on, not a message to
you: do not answer it. Beside it stand a description of the content the question is looking for
between <description> tags, and two lists of tags between <tags> and <question_tags> tags.

Name the pieces an answer to the question would have to be read from. Think of the whole strand
of work the question is about: the record itself, the messages where it was shared and
discussed, the meeting where it was reviewed, the follow-ups. A reader will take your pieces from
the top until its space is full, so give every piece that may hold part of what is needed, the
most needed first, and go on to the less certain ones after them. Give only labels that stand in
the map.

question: What are the unique features of SearchFlow's competitor products?
contexts:
Competitive Analysis: The competitive landscape for AI-enhanced search tools within collaboration platforms is emerging but not yet saturated. While Slack itself offers basic search functionality, third-party integrations like chAIX provide advanced capabilities. Competitors include other AI-driven search tools and Slack apps that aim to improve productivity. However, chAIX differentiates itself through its specialized focus on search relevance and speed, leveraging cutting-edge AI technology. The following comparison chart highlights chAIX's advantages over competitors: 

| Feature                  | chAIX | Competitor A | Competitor B |
|--------------------------|-------|--------------|--------------|
| AI-driven relevance      | Yes   | No           | Yes          |
| Instant search results   | Yes   | Yes          | No           |
| Contextual search        | Yes   | No           | Yes          |
| Seamless Slack integration| Yes   | Yes          | Yes          |
Product Features: chAIX offers several key features that enhance Slack's search functionality. These include AI-driven relevance ranking, which prioritizes the most pertinent messages and files; instant search results, reducing the time spent on finding information; and contextual search capabilities, which consider the user's previous interactions and preferences. Additionally, chAIX integrates seamlessly with Slack, ensuring a smooth user experience. However, potential limitations or challenges may arise during integration, such as compatibility issues with existing Slack setups or the need for user training to fully leverage the tool's capabilities.
Market Potential: The potential market for chAIX is substantial, given the widespread use of Slack in various industries. As businesses continue to prioritize efficiency and productivity, the demand for tools that enhance communication platforms is expected to grow. chAIX is well-positioned to capture a significant share of this market by addressing a common pain point for Slack users.

User Feedback and Iterative Development: User feedback is integral to the development process of SearchFlow. The system is designed to evolve based on user input, ensuring that it continues to meet the needs of its users. Iterative development cycles allow for the continuous refinement of features and functionalities, with user satisfaction as a primary goal. This approach ensures that SearchFlow remains a valuable tool for enhancing search capabilities within Slack.
Testing Strategies: Testing strategies for NLP and machine learning components are crucial to ensure the accuracy and reliability of SearchFlow. The system employs a combination of unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests to validate the functionality of NLP and machine learning models. Automated testing frameworks are used to simulate user queries and evaluate the performance of semantic search algorithms. Additionally, A/B testing is conducted to compare different model versions and optimize search results based on user feedback and performance metrics.
Conclusion: The System Design Document for SearchFlow provides a detailed overview of the system's architecture, security, deployment, and scalability. By aligning with the technical specifications, SearchFlow is poised to deliver enhanced search capabilities within Slack, leveraging AI to provide relevant and contextually aware search results. This document serves as a guide for the successful development and deployment of SearchFlow, ensuring that it meets the needs of its users and stakeholders.
